Text: From Barbedwire Studios and Digitalmindsoft,   We want to thank all the participants in the CtA - Gates of Hell: Ostfront beta test   for all your feedback and the playtime invested.  Join our Discord. Our goal is to build a strong community around our game  See you in the battlefield, commanders!

Hello everyone, we’re back with more information about the upcoming DLCs, and we have an anniversary to celebrate with you! 10 years of Barbedwire Studios!  We think we have one of the most loyal, knowledgeable and helpful communities in the world of gaming. And so, it’s time for us to give something in return!  As a celebration of our history we will be releasing the Jubilee DLC, a free small addition to the game that will contain bonus missions, nostalgic locations and assets, and  a bunch of easter eggs.   In June 2021 we put the final release date on our project and decided to keep our free playtest running until the very end, fully confident that we would launch with the appraisal of the community. Today, 4 years later, we reaffirm our commitment and our passion for our project.

Welcome back to the battlefield, Soldiers. New update 60 inbound!  We have optimized <c(f5d167)>MULTIPLAYER</c> memory consumption and loading times, more <c(f5d167)>ANIMATION</c> improvements, new features to control your vehicle's <c(f5d167)>REVERSE</c> motion, and more!.   Thank you for your continued support.

We have just released Content Update 6, one of our biggest updates thus far!  It covers <c(f5d167)>CONQUEST</c> improvements, <c(f5d167)>ANTI-AIRCRAFT</c> fixes, <c(f5d167)>OPTIMIZATION</c>, new <c(f5d167)>ANIMATIONS</c>, and a MASSIVE addition of content to the <c(f5d167)>TALVISOTA DLC</c>.  We're grateful that you enable us to keep updating the game and working with the community to make these improvements come true.   We'd like to thank our volunteer helpers and the supporter pack owners for going the extra mile to make this happen. If you'd like to see continued updates to our older releases, please consider joining the fight by acquring the <c(f5d167)>SUPPORTER PACK</c>.

The long wait is almost over! The <c(f5d167)>COMMONWEALTH</c> is coming!  A few words from the Prime Minister, Mr. Churchill:  What General Weygand called the Battle of France is over. I expect that the Battle of Britain is about to begin. The whole fury and might of the enemy must very soon be turned on us.   Let us therefore brace ourselves to our duties, and so bear ourselves that if the British Empire and its Commonwealth last for a thousand years, men will still say, <c(f5d167)>'THIS WAS THEIR FINEST HOUR'</c>.

The long awaited release is finally here! The <c(f5d167)>COMMONWEALTH</c> forces have arrived to the battlefield! It is not only our biggest production to date, but it also adds a <c(f5d167)>whole new level of detail and cinematography to the singleplayer experience</c>.  'Finest Hour' tells the story of the British commonwealth forces in western Europe, the Polish forces in exile, and the German invasion of France and eventual retreat.   'We shall fight in France, we shall fight on the seas and oceans, we shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air, we shall defend our Island, whatever the cost may be, we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; <c(f5d167)>we shall never surrender!</c>.'

Play more, wait less.   Jump into Ranked PvP 1v1 & 2v2 or Casual queues with quick MMR-matched opponents. No more dead lobbies. No more getting kicked. Just nonstop games.   Join our Discord Now! Go to -  <c(f5d167)>Channels & Roles- Ranked PvP role</c> - and join in on the fun!

Yet another highly anticipated update for our dynamic campaign generator, Conquest, is here!   Smarter AI, dug-in defensive positions, community-requested changes, retreating mechanics and devastating counterattacks.  Update 70 also brings you sound optimizations, and much more!   <c(f5d167)>We're running a special sale to celebrate this important milestone!</c>

Using his rifle a sniper can eliminate enemy personnel from a safe distance and spot hiding enemy saboteurs using the rifle's mounted telescopic sight. Camouflage is the sniper's main weapon. That is why, in addition to his scoped Springfield rifle, he carries a throwing knife and several camouflaging bushes.

One of the most widely used British cruiser tanks entered mass production in January 1943 and was the modified version of the Crusader tank. The turret-mounted 75mm gun was unable to penetrate frontal armor of the newest German tanks, however the Mk.VIII Cromwell was respected by tank crews for its speed and manoeuvrability. The tank was designed for quick penetration deep into enemy territory and strategic initiative support.

When one of the frontline divisions achieved corageous success in the ongoing battles, the USSR high command granted them the honorary position of Guards of the Soviet Union. They were prioritised when considering the operation battle plans, likewise they were usually better equipped. <c(DB465A)>Soviet Guard divisions have more experience in battle and better equipment than regular regular infantry, and they carry a MG in the squad for suppession.</c>

A team of six soldiers, each armed with two anti-personnel grenades and a Mauser rifle. The rifle's long range make the squad most effective over long and medium distances. However, due to the Mauser's low-capacity cartridge and a low rate of fire, at close range those riflemen are easy targets for submachine gunners and assault infantry.

Soviet Paratroopers of the start of WW2 saw action in the Winter War and in several behind enemy line operations of WW2. They are, therefore, trained for versatile operations that include sabotage, assassination, combat, etc. <c(DB465A)>Soviet Paratroopers are a compromise between sabotage and frontline combat. They are semi-stealthy and carry deadly satchels and molotovs, but they also wield light semi-automatic weapons for short to medium range encounters. They also sprint faster to be able to be able to ensure swift 'boom and zooms'. To fully maaximise their potential they do require careful micro-control.</c>

The Universal Carrier, also known (incorrectly) as the Bren Gun Carrier is a common name describing a family of light armored tracked vehicles built by Vickers-Armstrong. Produced between 1934 and 1960, the vehicle was used widely by British Commonwealth forces during the Second World War. Universal Carriers were usually used for transporting personnel and equipment, mostly support weapons, or as machine gun platforms. With some 113,000 built in the United Kingdom and abroad, it was the most produced armored fighting vehicle in history

In the inventory of these trucks you will find armor-piercing and high explosive rounds, crates to carry them, and a repair kit.   This army truck was an upgraded version of the civilian ACX-353. During the war these vehicles were used for transporting cargo, relocating troops towing artillery. Some modifications could be used as gasoline tankers.

Entered service with the German army in 1942 and was considered the best tank until the end of 1943. Soviet 45mm guns could not penetrate the Tiger's armor even at point-blank range, while its 88mm gun was able to destroy any tank of the times.

Anti-tank minefields are primarily meant for securing troop deployment zones from enemy vehicles and tanks and are mainly used in front of occupied positions or to guard one's flanks. A group of four mine laying specialists is armed with Thompson submachine guns and is capable of quickly laying minefields, thereby securing disputed or strategically important sectors.

A soldier armed with a flame-thrower can inflict heavy damage on infantry inside a building and can single-handedly clear an entire area of enemies. In spite of this, he is extremely vulnerable because once he has used up all of his flammable liquid he remains unarmed and a random bullet can cause an explosion if it hits his cylinder. Accordingly, a combat unit includes several escort submachine gunners.

A group of four mine laying specialists is armed with MP-40 submachine guns and is capable of quickly laying minefields, thereby securing disputed or strategically important sectors.

A group of four mine laying specialists is armed with MP-40 submachine guns and is capable of quickly laying minefields, thereby securing disputed or strategically important sectors.

The portable anti-tank rocket launcher Bazooka was designed to fight enemy equipment and could actually put any tank out of action if used skilfully. The damage capacity of a high-explosion grenade is not reduced over distance, but rocket launchers are still most efficient at close and medium range. It is very difficult to hit a target when firing a Bazooka at long range. An infantryman carrying a rocket launcher is extremely vulnerable which is why a combat unit includes a submachine gunner to escort and cover him.

Boys AT, the British anti-tank rifle, was adopted in November 1937. Since its killing power was rather low – a 60-gram bullet could pierce up to 15mm of armor – such rifles were only used against light-armored targets. This rifle couldn't destroy a medium or heavy tank, it could only knock off a track or damage a gun.

The saboteur is a well-trained soldier capable of single-handedly inflicting devastating damage on the enemy. He can hide in bushes or tall grass and stay almost invisible while crawling. He is armed with a silenced pistol, several throwing knives, an incendiary grenade and an explosive charge powerful enough to turn the heaviest tanks into a heap of scrap metal.

The light infantry composes the basic structure of Soviet rushed recruitment and deployment of troops during WW2. <c(DB465A)>The squad leader carries a sub-machinegun and a few grenades while the standard squad members have ordinary rifles.</c>]

The Volkssturm were civilians armed with small amounts of ammunition and cheap weaponry, including the infamous Panzerfaust AT shaped charge rockets, with the purpose of being the last line of defense of the Fatherland. They composed a weak but nonetheless relevant defense, inflicting damage upon the advancing troops in Germany at the end of the war. The command of these groups fell in the hands of the SS and Nazi political figureheards, significantly reducing it's potential as an efficient fighting force.<c(DB465A)> They are a good last resort unit for desperate measures, but do not expect miracles from these troops.</c>

The Vickers medium machine gun appeared in 1912 in Great Britain as a modification of the famous Maxim gun and was used by the British Army until the 1960s. The machine gun offered an excellent rate of fire at long range but its heavy weight made transportation difficult.

The Pioniere squads are the top of the Wehrmacht infantry spearhead, and they were greately respected and admired by the High Command. <c(DB465A)>They carry flamethrowers, grenades and other demolition equipment. Their specialty: Dealing with the enemy frontline fortifications face to face. Provided they can reach the enemy strongholds through the open ground, mayhem shall spread as the demolitions begin.

The first production models of a new infantry support tank appeared in June 1941. The design was to replace the Mk.II "Matilda", which was quickly becoming obsolete, but due to a short development cycle it was sent to production with a range of defects. The tank had a low profile and strong armor, but its extremely weak armament negated these advantages. Further modifications did not help - a newly mounted 75mm gun did not improve its anti-tank capabilities leaving the Mk.IV with the role of an infantry support vehicle.

In the time of the German invasion of the USSR, the borders were often guarded by border militia. They were part of the Army, yet they were not trained nor armed as much as regular army forces. Some of them wore civilian clothing<c(DB465A)>Their simple armament consisting of rifles without additional grenades nor automatic weapons makes them adequate at medium to long range encounters, but by all means they are not trained to engage any elite infantry that opposes it. Use them strategically to cover holes in your defense line, their low price and low CP enables them to be fielded easily.</c>]

In 1942, Great Britain started manufacturing its own anti-tank rocket launchers to replace its inefficient anti-tank rifles. A shaped charge fired from a PIAT could burn through a 120mm armor plate, allowing it to destroy almost any enemy vehicle. Since firing accuracy was greatly reduced at long distances, rocket launchers were most effective at close and medium range. An infantryman armed with a rocket launcher was very vulnerable. For this reason, such a squad also included a submachine gunner to cover him.

The presence of a veteran officer on the battlefield can turn the course of any battle. Using his field binoculars he can spot enemy infantry and saboteurs hiding in bushes and tall grass. The officer can also spot enemy units at a distance allowing you to regroup and react ahead of time. Besides his binoculars, he also carries a knife and a Nagant pistol. These weapons are poorly suited for a heated battle.

The Luftwaffe field units were deployed to give frontline support to the Wehrmacht as well as protecting the airfields on the combat zone from land raids. <c(DB465A)>They are not the most resilient of soldiers and they are not trained like other elites, but they are staggeringly deadly with their choice of equipment: AT weaponry against enemy vehicles and aircraft-based MG15's, which provide second-to-none accurate suppression. A great unit for defensive means.</c>
Sturmpioniere are motorised Pioneers under the command of the Panzerwaffe (Tank corps). <c(DB465A)>They come on board a Hanomag.</c>

Anti-tank minefields are primarily meant for securing troop deployment sites and are mainly placed before the occupied position, occasionally on the flanks. A group of four mine-laying specialists is armed with MP-40 submachine guns and capable of quickly deploying the obstacle line, thereby securing disputable or strategically important sectors.

The effectiveness of a tank depends first of all on the cohesion of the crew and its ability to act consistently in any situation. The most powerful and dangerous machine will become just a pile of scrap if the people controlling it suddenly disappear. When training a tank crew, complete cross-training of all members is key because the tank must remain battle-worthy even if only one crew member survives...   Although tank crews are armed with compact MP-40 submachine guns, they have no combat training and are hence extremely vulnerable.

The Brandenburger commandos were stealth units trained in foreign languages, combat and demolition tasks. They were fielded during the war for the most perilous undercover tasks, from detonating bridges and sabotaging the enemy to switching the entire road directions on the enemy territory to confuse the foes. <c(DB465A)>They carry detonation equipment and good weaponry, and they are both fast runners and stealthy.</c>

The Fallschirmjger (paratroopers) were considered the best german combat-trained unit and during the war they single-handedly undertook operations such as the assault of fort Eban-Emael, the capture of Crete and the defense of Monte-Cassino. After the capture of Crete, Hitler ordered no more large scale paradropping operations in risk of loosing too many of his elite.<c(DB465A)> They are solid all-round, and their squads incorporate from MG gunners to snipers. Towards the end of the war they became even more lethal with FG-42 automatic rifles and Panzerfausts.</c>

The German Gebirgsjger were mountain troops prepared to face the enemy on the most troublesome terrain and perilous circumstances. Their unrivaled strong point is that they train to be able to travel long distances without rest. Wherever they are sent to, they will arrive quickly and ready for combat wielding their Edelweiss emblem.<c(DB465A)> They are equipped with lighter rifles and their main man carries an MG34 with a double drum configuration, able to unload double the ammunition in every reload.</c>

Anti-tank minefields are primarily meant for securing troop deployment zones from enemy vehicles and tanks and are mainly used in front of occupied positions or to guard one's flanks. A group of four mine laying specialists is armed with PPSh submachine guns and is capable of quickly laying minefields, thereby securing disputed or strategically important sectors.

The MG-34 entered service with the Wehrmacht in 1934 and was used in hand, mounted, anti-aircraft and tank variants. An MG mounted on a tripod was able to fire at both ground and airborne targets. While it surpassed its Western counterparts in terms of rate of fire, continuous fire caused the machine gun's barrel to overheat quickly.

The SS grenadiers formed a reliable bulk of the german forces on the late years of the war and they were prepared to receive any orders. The fresh SS troops of 1944-45 were lightly trained but their impact on combat came down to having received the best armament the german industry was rushing, including STG-44 assault rifles and Panzerfaust anti-tank weapons. <c(DB465A)>They form a compact squad which is versatile in combat, able to attack, hold positions with sustained fire, and destroy enemy tanks.</c>

The Ausf.G Panther version was created as a response to the Soviet T34, and entered mass production in March 1944. Its relatively good manoeuvrability and a long-barrelled 75mm gun made the tank a dangerous adversary. Its insufficient side protection was compensated with excellent frontal armor.

Anti-tank minefields are primarily meant for securing troop deployment zones from enemy vehicles and tanks and are mainly used in front of occupied positions or to guard one's flanks. A group of four mine laying specialists is armed with MP-40 submachine guns and is capable of quickly laying minefields, thereby securing disputed or strategically important sectors.

Soviet heavy artillery field howitzer of 152mm calibre, capable of high Explosive and smoke rounds.   The 152mm howitzer entered service with the Red Army on August 8th, 1943. It was designed for indirect firing at enemy personnel, fortifications and trench lines. The D-1 was considered equal to world's best guns of its class and its mobility, range and the destructive force of high-explosive rounds have made it an almost perfect weapon of its times. On the battlefield it earned its reputation for being a reliable and accurate artillery piece boasting excellent ballistic characteristics and high mobility.

Entered service with the Wehrmacht in 1944. Its turret-mounted 88mm long-barrelled gun was capable of destroying any enemy tank from a long distance. In combination with its excellent armor, this made the King Tiger the most powerful tank of WWII. The Pz VI ausf.B is almost invulnerable to enemy guns, but its 70t weight has negative impact on its mobility.

The portable rocket launcher Bazooka was developed by US designers to fight enemy equipment. Some of them were delivered to the Soviet Union under the Lend-Lease program. Although the damage capacity of a high-explosion grenade is not reduced over distance, rocket launchers are most efficient at close and medium range. It is very difficult to hit a target when firing a bazooka at long range. An infantryman carrying a rocket launcher is extremely vulnerable which is why a combat unit includes a submachine gunner to cover him.

Soldiers are armed with MP-40 submachine guns, clusters of MP24 grenades to fight armored vehicles and several anti-personnel fragmentation grenades. Such squads are highly effective at fighting enemy infantry at close and medium range and accordingly can be used both to storm enemy positions and to repel enemy attacks.

Partisans were civilians armed with weapons from home, the enemy or dead comrades. They stood up against the German invasion and are willying to fight until the last breath for their burnt villages or dead families. <c(DB465A)>They are not trained for face to face combat unlike the army troops but they are ideal for ambushes, surprise attacks and they are inexpensive.</c>

This German anti-tank rifle was put into service with the Wehrmacht in 1939 and was the main infantry combat tool against light armored equipment before Panzerfausts were introduced. Its 14.5g bullet with tungsten core could pierce a 20mm armored plate when shot at medium range. This enabled the Panzerbushe 39 to establish en excellent reputation at the beginning of World War 2. However, with the advent of Matildas and T-34 the effectiveness of the rifle dropped significantly because at best it could only knock the tracks from these tanks or damage their guns. An anti-armor crew consists of two people.

Anti-tank minefields are primarily meant for securing troop deployment sites and are mainly placed in front of established positions and occasionally on the flanks. A group of four mine-laying specialists, armed with M3A1 submachine guns, is capable of quickly deploying the obstacle line, thereby securing unoccupied or strategically important sectors.

In 1941, the NKVD started recruiting criminals or convicted men in the USSR to form the infamous penal batallions. The convicts were given a chance to clean their crimes with blood by advancing into the enemy territory in massive suicidal attacks. Upon retreating, they would also get shot from their own NKVD commanders. <c(DB465A)>These troops are not very well armed and they do not carry plenty of ammunition. What counts is their sheer numbers and the ability to deploy them without extensive costs.</c>

The Heavy infantry squad was what the Soviet doctrines of the war demanded as the standard, but due to the constant losses and disorganisation after the sudden German invasion, the squads were often not fully fledged as per what was written on the book.<c(DB465A)>Heavy or full squads incorporate a MG gunner with it's assistant and thus grants a good suppression tool against the enemy compared to the light infantry.</c>

Anti-personnel minefields are intended to deny enemy personnel entry to deployment sites and are mainly placed in front of established positions or on the flanks. A group of four mine-laying soldiers, armed with M3A1 submachine guns, is capable of quick deployment of minefields, thereby securing unoccupied or strategically important sectors.

Anti-personnel minefields are intended to deny enemy personnel entry to deployment sites and are usually used in front of occupied positions or to guard one's flanks. A group of four mine-laying specialists is armed with PPSh submachine guns and is capable of quickly laying minefields, thereby securing disputed or strategically important sectors.

The Tortoise was the result of a heavy assault tank development process that began in Britain in 1942. Its heavy weight impaired its mobility, but it was decided that speed did not play a major role during the clearing of fortified positions. The hull, composed of rolled armor plates, could multiple direct hits and its upgraded anti-aircraft gun could successfully defeat German tanks. However, due to its long development cycle the A39 did not see action in WWII.

Anti-personnel minefields are intended to deny enemy personnel entry to deployment sites and are usually used in front of occupied positions or to guard one's flanks. A group of four mine-laying specialists is armed with Thompson submachine guns and is capable of quickly laying minefields, thereby securing disputed or strategically important sectors.

Production of this light off-road vehicle began in 1940. Thanks to its simplicity and reliability, the Kubelwagen soon added its name to the list of the most famous vehicles of World War 2, becoming one of the symbols of the German Army. Its air-cooled engine worked as well in hot African conditions as in freezing Russia, while its low vehicle weight had a positive effect on its cross-country ability. Some modifications were equipped with a vertical bar with a machine gun mount.

The Hummel self-propelled heavy 150mm howitzer entered service with the Wehrmacht in May 1943 and was designed to demolish enemy fortifications and provide support to assault groups. Its low ordnance capacity along with thin, open-top armor made it unsuitable for close combat. In spite of this, the "Bumblebee" was a fearsome weapon, capable of dealing tremendous damage to the enemy.

The portable anti-tank Panzerschreck was an expensive but powerful weapon, vastly superior to the American Bazooka in terms of its piercing performance. The damage capacity of a high-explosion grenade is not reduced over distance but rocket launchers are still most efficient at close and medium range. It is very difficult to hit a target when firing such a weapon at long range. An infantry man carrying a rocket launcher is extremely vulnerable which is why a combat unit includes an escort submachine gunner.

This anti-tank rifle designed by Simonov entered service with the Red Army on 29 August, 1941 and was put into mass production shortly afterwards. It differed from other models due to its increased weight and self-loading feed system. In the early days of the war, this weapon was used to fight all types of German equipment but over time its effectiveness dropped noticeably. In the later stages of the war an anti-tank rifle could no longer destroy medium and heavy enemy tanks but was only able to damage their tracks and guns. A PTRS crew consists of two people.

Commando special purpose troops were formed at Churchill's initiative in June 1940 for reconnaissance and sabotage actions in the enemy's rear and for the most critical assault operations. Commandos were armed with American Thompson submachine guns, Bren light machine guns as well as smoke, anti-personnel and anti-tank grenades. Commando squads were considered elite by right – their excellent training and impressive arsenal guaranteed effective military action in all conditions.

German airborne troops came into being in 1935 and took part in a number of assault operations at the beginning of World War 2. Unlike similar units in other countries, German paratroopers did not belong to the special forces and were, as a matter of fact, well-trained infantry operating in the air. Those fearless fighters were armed with anti-tank, anti-personnel and smoke grenades, dynamite sticks, knives, submachine guns and FG 42 assault rifles which enabled them to fight effectively in all conditions.

Red Banner marine battalions were staffed with sailors and officers of the USSR Navy. Those brave and tough soldiers were sent to the most dangerous areas of the front where the harsh battles they fought made them deserving of the status of Soviet elite troops. Marines are fearless and well armed. Their self-loading rifles designed by Tokarev boast an excellent firing rate and the large number of anti-tank, anti-personnel and smoke grenades available to them enables them to effectively fight in all conditions.

Ranger units were developed in the USA in 1942 to perform reconnaissance and sabotage tasks in the Pacific and in Africa. They could be landed by air or sea while their arsenal included anti-tank, anti-personnel and smoke grenades, M1A1 semi-automatic carbines, Thompson submachine guns and dynamite sticks. These armaments enabled special forces to fight effectively both in the enemy’s rear and on the front line.

A soldier armed with a flame-thrower can inflict heavy damage on infantry inside a building and can single-handedly clear an entire area of enemies. In spite of this, he is extremely vulnerable because once he has used up all of his flammable liquid he remains unarmed and a random bullet can cause an explosion if it hits his cylinder. Accordingly, a combat unit includes several escort submachine gunners.

In spite of this, he is extremely vulnerable because once he has used up all of his flammable liquid he remains unarmed and a random bullet can cause an explosion if it hits his cylinder. Accordingly, a combat unit includes several escort submachine gunners.

A combat team of two soldiers armed with Bren light machine guns can provide excellent fire support to friendly infantry on assault. The Bren's low magazine capacity is made up for by its high rate of fire and killing power. In addition, when mounted on special supports to fire from under cover or from a prone position, its accuracy and density of fire is greatly improved.

Combining excellent rate of fire, high firepower and large cartridge capacity, the MG42 is a dangerous weapon against enemy infantry and provides much-needed fire support to advancing friendly troops. While firing from cover or prone position, the weapon is put on a special mount which significantly increase its accuracy.

High stopping power and rate of fire make the Degtyaryov light machine-gun an ideal weapon for providing fire cover, at the same time turning each machine gunner into a formidable opponent to all enemy personnel. When firing from defilade or prone position, the weapon is placed on a special mount, which dramatically increases its accuracy.

A combat team of two soldiers armed with Browning Automatic Rifles can provide excellent fire support for advancing friendly infantry. Low cartridge capacity is more than compensated by a high rate of fire and the B.A.R.'s stopping power. Firing it from a mounted position results in a significant increase in accuracy.

The presence of a seasoned officer on the battlefield can change the course of battle. Using field binoculars, he can spot enemy infantry and saboteurs hiding in bushes or long grass. An officer can also spot an enemy from a long distance allowing time to regroup and react. As well as binoculars, he carries a knife and a personal handgun. However, these weapons are not suited to a heated battle.

The presence of a veteran officer on the battlefield can turn the course of any battle. Using his field binoculars he can spot enemy infantry and saboteurs hiding in bushes and tall grass. The officer can also spot enemy units at a distance allowing you to regroup and react ahead of time. Besides his binoculars, he also carries a knife and a Walther pistol. These weapons are poorly suited for a heated battle.

The presence of a veteran officer on the battlefield can turn the course of any battle. Using his field binoculars he can spot enemy infantry and saboteurs hiding in bushes and tall grass. The officer can also spot enemy units at a distance allowing you to regroup and react ahead of time. Besides his binoculars, he also carries a knife and a Colt pistol. These weapons are poorly suited for a heated battle.

A squad of six British infantrymen armed with a few anti-personnel grenades and EM-3 rifles. These riflemen are most effective at long and medium ranges. In close combat, they become easy prey for enemy submachine gunners and assault squads.

A team of six privates, each armed with two anti-personnel grenades and a standard-issue Mosin rifle. The rifle's long range make the squad most effective over long and medium distances. However, due to the Mosin's low-capacity cartridge and a comparatively low rate of fire, at close range those riflemen are easy targets for submachine gunners and assault infantry.

A squad of six American infantrymen armed with several anti-personnel grenades and Springfield rifles. Riflemen are most efficient at long and medium range. In close combat they are easy prey for enemy submachine gunners and assault squads.

The design of this 81mm gun closely follows its Soviet counterpart, consisting of three main sections: firing tube, support plate and a two-legged mount. It fires 3,5kg HE rounds via indirect trajectory. Firing is triggered by the pin inside the tube striking the primer of a descending shell.
A single unit of these, can turn enemy tanks into scrapmetal easely. This unit is perfect for stealth attacking the enemy's outpost.
Univeral Tractor. Common in the countryside in the 40s.

This American medium tank entered mass production in 1942 and, from then on, was widely used in all the theatres of war. It was supplied in large quantities to the US allies under the Lend-Lease program. Thanks to its fully cast hull and thick armor, the M4A1 was no weaker than the Soviet T-34 series while having superior ergonomics, more space inside the turret and good speed. Its 75mm gun performed well, hitting enemy light and medium equipment but, after the advent of Tigers and Panthers, it lost its former effectiveness.

Using portable mine detectors, this two-man squad of skilled demolition specialists can quickly detect and clear any minefields. Disarmed mines may be picked up and reused. For front-line operations, the squad is armed with Sten Mk.1 submachine guns and can offer some resistance. Nevertheless, it is not recommended that these specialists be sent to attack fortified enemy positions.

Using portable mine detectors a two-man squad of skilled demolition experts can quickly detect and clear any minefields. A disarmed mine may then be picked up and reused. To deal with enemy encounters the squad is armed with MP-40 submachine guns. While they can defend themselves, it is not recommended to send these specialists to attack fortified enemy positions.

This Sherman tank modification was built in 1942 for clearing the minefields with a special mine flail. The engine-powered, spinning rotor was mounted in front of the vehicle on two arms. The rotor had steel chains with balls attached to it. The rotation caused the chains to hit the ground, exploding all mines in front of the vehicle. The turret of these tanks was often removed, and they were left with only a machine gun for defence.

Using portable mine detectors a two-man squad of skilled demolition experts can quickly detect and clear any minefields. A disarmed mine may then be picked up and reused. To deal with enemy encounters the squad is armed with PPSh submachine guns. While they can defend themselves, it is not recommended to send these specialists to attack fortified enemy positions.

The most powerful of all US Army tank destroyers entered mass production in November 1943. Its chassis was taken from its predecessor - the self-propelled M10A1 anti-tank gun. The good armor penetration capabilities of the modified 90mm gun mounted on the "Slugger" allowed it to hold its own against heavy German tanks. Its thick frontal armor protected it from enemy shells and its good maneuverability compensated for its only serious flaw - an open turret that left its crew vulnerable.

Using portable mine detectors a two-man squad of skilled demolition experts can quickly detect and clear any minefields. A disarmed mine may then be picked up and reused. To deal with enemy encounters the squad is armed with Thompson submachine guns. While they can defend themselves, it is not recommended to send these specialists to attack fortified enemy positions.

An SAS operative is capable of single-handedly inflicting devastating damage on the enemy. He can crawl without being noticed and can spy on enemy positions, staying out of sight. He is armed with a silenced De Lisle carbine, throwing knives and a few explosive charges powerful enough to turn a heavy enemy tank into a useless pile of metal.

This soldier has received his training in the best German intelligence schools, and is capable of inflicting devastating damage to the enemy single-handedly. He can hide from enemy sight in bushes or tall grass, and become almost invisible while crawling. He is armed with a silenced pistol, several throwing knives, and a couple of dynamite sticks for destroying heavily-armored vehicles.

The most powerful and dangerous machine will become just a pile of scrap if the people controlling it suddenly disappear. When training a tank crew, complete cross-training of all members is key because the tank must remain battle-worthy even if only one crew member survives...   Although Soviet tank crews are armed with compact PPS-43 submachine guns, they have no combat training and are hence extremely vulnerable.

US Army marine squads are most suitable for special operations involving the capture of strategic locations. They are armed with Garand rifles, Browning automatic rifles, anti-personnel, smoke and anti-tank grenades. Such special force fighters are most effective at long and medium range while steel breastplates protect fighters from small splinters and random bullets.

The saboteur is a well-trained soldier capable of single-handedly inflicting devastating damage on the enemy. He can hide in bushes or tall grass and stay almost invisible while crawling. He is armed with a silenced pistol, several throwing knives, an incendiary grenade and an explosive charge powerful enough to turn the heaviest tanks into a heap of scrap metal.

Sub-machine gunners are armed with Sten Mk.1 guns, anti-personnel, anti-tank and smoke grenades. A squad of six submachine gunners can be used in both defence and offence and can effectively fight enemy infantry at close and medium ranges.

A squad of six soldiers, each armed with a PPSh submachine gun, several AP grenades and a RPG-40 anti-tank grenade. The PPSh is equipped with a large-capacity drum cartridge, which holds 71 rounds of ammo, and is especially effective at close and medium ranges. This six-man group may be used for assaulting enemy positions or guarding tanks and field guns.

In the skilled hands of a sniper, a Mauser 98K rifle can eliminate enemy personnel from long distances. The mounted telescopic sight allows the sniper to spot hidden enemy saboteurs. Camouflage is the sniper's main weapon, that's why in addition to the telescope-sighted rifle he carries a throwing knife and several camouflaging bushes.

These soldiers are armed with a Thompson submachine gun, a couple of anti-personnel grenades and an No.73 anti-tank grenade. A combat unit of six submachine gunners may be successfully used for both defence and attack tasks. It can effectively fight enemy infantry at close and medium range.

Using his rifle, a sniper can eliminate enemy personnel from a safe distance and the mounted telescopic sight allows him to spot even the best-hidden enemy saboteurs. Camouflage is the sniper's main weapon which is why, in addition to a telescope-sighted EM-2 rifle, he carries a throwing knife and several camouflaging bushes.

Using his rifle a sniper can eliminate enemy personnel from a safe distance and spot hiding enemy saboteurs using the rifle's mounted telescopic sight. Camouflage is the sniper's main weapon. That is why, in addition to his scoped Mosin rifle, he carries a throwing knife and several camouflaging bushes.

The British assault troops were made up of physically strong, young soldiers who were given additional training before being sent on the most difficult and critical of missions – from assaulting standalone weapon emplacements to securing defence lines and permanent fortifications. Such troops were armed with American submachine guns and British Bren light machine guns. Their arsenals also included dynamite sticks, anti-personnel, anti-tank and smoke grenades. Special steel breastplates were used as protection from bullets and shell fragments.

The elite units of the Wehrmacht are well trained and equipped. A squad of six heavy infantrymen is ideal for storming enemy positions and capturing strategic points. The squad’s arsenal includes MP-44 submachine guns, Panzerfaust grenade launchers, smoke, anti-personnel and high-explosive anti-tank grenades. Most effective at close and medium combat range where a metal breastplate will protect a heavy infantryman from rifle bullets.

Assault engineer brigades were introduced in May 1943 by order of the Headquarters of the Supreme High Command for the purpose of breaking through fortified enemy defensive lines and fighting in urban environments. A squad of six such soldiers is most suitable for storming enemy defensive lines and capturing strategic points. The squad is armed with Sudaev submachine guns, high-explosion anti-tank RPG43 grenades, petrol bombs, dynamite and smoke and anti-personnel grenades. Most effective at close and medium combat range where a metal breastplate will protect a heavy infantryman from rifle bullets.

The Geman volksgrenadiers, cheap and voluntery units like these, were only given a gun, a helmet and a uniform and often sent straight towards the frontline.

Shermans entered mass production in 1942. Despite being the strongest US tank at the time it could not compete with German tanks - its high profile and weak armor along with the poor performance of its main gun contributed to the overall vulnerability of the tank. Nevertheless, thanks to the relatively low costs of production, the Sherman functioned as the main battle tank of the Allies.

In the inventory of these trucks you will found fuel canisters, repair kits, ammunition, grenades and other ordnance.   This army truck was an upgrade of the civilian vehicle ACX-353. During the war, these vehicles were often used to transport cargo, relocate troops and tow artillery. Some modifications could have been used as a fuel trucks.

Inside this truck you will find tools for repairing equipment, materials for building obstacles and defences and anti-personnel and anti-tank mines. Obstacles are usually built in front of occupied positions or sometimes on the flanks and in the gaps between them. Defences are made of sandbags and serve to strengthen the positions of friendly infantry.   The Opel Blitz was a reliable and undemanding vehicle and was widely used in World War 2. It was perfect for the harsh conditions of military action and had many roles, from ambulance to mobile headquarters. Suitable for the fast redeployment of troops on a mass scale and for towing artillery.

In 1944, British engineers created Achilles, the improved tank destroyer based on the American M10 Wolverine Gun Motor Carriage. Essentially, it had a long-barrelled QF17 gun of premium armor-piercing performance mounted on the chassis of the M4A2 Sherman main battle tank. While providing excellent mobility, this also made it impossible to install durable armor plating.

In an effort to provide mobile anti-tank artillery support to their attacking infantry, the British Army placed an order with Vickers to develop a new self-propelled gun that would meet all the modern warfare requirements of the time. First produced in 1944, Archers had an original design: their long-barrelled 76mm QF17 guns were capable of fighting any German tank, but their back to front position proved very inconvenient during offensives.

Development of this tank was begun by AEC in August 1943. Within 2 years, it was being mass produced and had become a masterpiece among the British armored vehicles of its time. The Centurion arrived too late for World War 2 but, had it happened, the German Panthers and Tigers would have had little or no chance of victory in a duel. The new vehicles had an excellent shell-proof capacity and their stabilised long-barrelled 76mm guns could quickly destroy almost any enemy.

Soviet mass-produced heavy armored car, able to engage enemy soft-skinned or lightly armored tanks and vehicles. Requires 3 crew.   The BA-11 is a heavily-armored vehicle mass produced since 1938 and mostly used as a mobile platform for providing fire support to advancing infantry. In comparison to some other light tanks, it boasted thicker armor, as well as higher manoeuvrability and firepower. An upgraded ZIS-16 engine allowed it to reach high speeds, while a turret-mounted 45mm gun could penetrate the armor of almost all light and medium tanks of its times.

This light 4WD armored car equipped with a machine gun was used by the Soviet Army from 1942 for the purposes of reconnaissance and protection in combat. Its bullet-proof armor could not protect the crew from even small-calibre rounds but its small size and high ride characteristics made the BA 64 a difficult target for enemy artillery.

In the inventory of these trucks you will find armor-piercing and high-explosive rounds, a box for transporting them and a repair kit.   The reliable and undemanding Bredfords were widely used by the British Army during World War 2. These 3-ton trucks carried infantry and cargo and towed artillery. They served as fuel trucks, hospital and command vehicles and mobile workshops.

Soviet all-purpose general machinegun, utilised by Infantry and Armored units alike.   The machine gun of Vasily Degtyaryov's design had been used by the Red Army since 1927 until the end of WWII. The weapon turned out to be quite a success. Safe and easy to use, demonstrating high rate of fire, it was superior to all existing machineguns and its place in the Red Army's arsenal was well-deserved.

The low efficiency of QF2 guns became obvious right after they were adopted leading Great Britain to begin development of a new anti-tank gun before World War 2. It was adopted 4 years later, replacing the obsolete 2-pounder. QF6 guns were successfully used in North Africa to destroy light and medium enemy tanks but they were incapable of penetrating the thick armor plates of the new Tigers and Panthers.

Inside these trucks you will find a petrol can, a repair kit, small arms ammo, grenades and other ammunition. They served as fuel trucks, hospital and command vehicles and mobile workshops.

These light field howitzers were in service with the American Army from 1930. Their design was aimed at making their dismantling and transportation as simple as possible because they were expected to be delivered by airborne gliders. Being relatively small in size, this modified 75mm gun was intended to offer direct fire support to airborne units and outperformed its counterparts in mobility and fire rate.
The 109 was the basic fighter in the German Luftwaffe, used in many places and is known for its agility and firepower.

A self-propelled howitzer mounted on the Valentine tank hull. Its main purpose was to provide the 25-pounder howitzer with a mobile platform. The hurried design process led to some flaws - the fixed turret turned out to be very tall, which in combination with the vehicle's low speed made it an ideal target. Despite this, the Bishop was successfully used as an infantry support weapon and siege gun.

Vickers 6 inch 26 cwt howitzer was developed in 1915 and, for a long time, served as the primary weapon of its class in the British Army. The high-explosive shells of the BL6 successfully eliminated enemy personnel and dealt significant damage to their fortifications. However, the lack of an armor plate made its crew very vulnerable.

Supply trucks carrying fuel canisters, repair kits, ammunition, grenades and other equipment.   Opel Blitz was a reliable and easy to maintain vehicle present in all theatres of WWII. It was ideally suited for harsh battlefield conditions and was used in different versions, from ambulance trucks to mobile HQs. The Blitz is perfect for transporting troops and towing artillery.

Suitable for the fast redeployment of troops on a mass scale and for towing artillery.

Soviet standard calibre Infantry field mortar, capable of high explosive, smoke and shrapnel rounds.   Developed in 1937, the Soviet 82mm mortar is a smooth-bore, indirect-fire grenade launcher used to engage enemy personnel and suppress its fortified emplacements. The weapon's construction follows the usual scheme: explosion is triggered by a fixed-pin primer mounted inside the shell; and a two-legged mount supports the firing tube, providing it with the required firing angle. Reliability, ease of use and mobility earned this weapon popularity amongst elite infantry troops.

The decree for mass production of the Katyusha was signed on June 21, 1941, and just three weeks later the rocket launcher appeared on the field of battle in Orsha. Guiding rails for launching M13 rockets were mounted atop a ZIS-6 truck, providing the vehicle with much required mobility. Their long range caused the rockets to scatter over a large area, making the weapon unsuitable for pinpoint attacks. Area strikes, on the other hand, were highly effective.

The Pz.Kpfw.III entered mass production in September 1939. One year later, it received improved armor, as well as a new long-barrelled 50mm gun. The tank was able to successfully engage and destroy armored cars and light tanks, although with the appearance of the T-34 it became largely obsolete.

The Browning was initially developed for air forces, but in 1923 another version was developed for ground forces as well. The upgraded version was dubbed M1919 and was widely used by the US Army. Its good rate of fire and effective range made it one of the most successful and widespread mounted machine guns in US Army service.

Soviet medium-light Infantry support tank, quick and agile, able to carry a squad of men into battle whilst also capable of dueling light tanks and vehicles.   BT (Bystrokhodny tank, meaning 'fast tank') was based on the 'convertible' M1931 Christie tank and produced in the USSR since 1935. Weighing 13.5 tonnes, this 'self-propelled gun' version was able to achieve high speeds, while retaining relatively thick armor, and high firepower thanks to its 76mm. The BT was designed for fast raids into enemy territory and quick offensive operations without infantry support.

The 8 cm Granatwerfer 34 (8 cm GrW 34) was the standard German medium mortar throughout World War II. It gained a reputation for extreme accuracy and rapid rate of fire, although much of the credit should go to the training of the crews.The design of the weapon was conventional and it broke down into three loads (barrel, bipod, baseplate) for transport. The barrel was smooth bore. Attached to its bipod were a traversing handwheel, and a cross-leveling handwheel below the elevating mechanism. A panoramic sight was mounted on the traversing mechanism yoke for fine adjustments. A line on the tube could be used for rough laying. The 8 cm GrW 34/1 was an adaptation for use in self-propelled mountings. A lightened version with a shorter barrel was put into production as the kurzer 8 cm Granatwerfer 42. The mortar employed conventional 8 cm 3.5 kg high explosive or smoke shells with percussion fuzes, having a range of just over a kilometer.

The ZSU self-propelled AA gun was created in 1942 on the chassis of  the "Crusader" cruiser tank. The chassis was left unchanged, but the standard turret was replaced with a purpose-built one, which housed two paired 20mm Oerlikon guns. The gun had an excellent rate of fire and could engage not only planes, but also lightly-armored ground targets and infantry. The insufficient armor was somewhat compensated for with good mobility.

In 1941, British Dodge began production of an all-wheel drive Weapon Carrier car ordered by the British military. The vehicle was larger than its American counterparts and had a more powerful engine and higher holding and carrying capacity. A special body mount allowed for the installation of a 37mm gun for battling light-armored enemy vehicles. A Vickers gun could also be installed to counter enemy personnel.

The Elefant tank destroyer entered service with the Wehrmacht in the spring of 1943. Its cabin-mounted 88mm gun was considered to be the deadliest weapon of its times and allowed the vehicle to destroy most enemy tanks from beyond their range of effective fire. Its armor - sometimes as thick as 200mm - made the Elefant impervious to frontal attacks, but due to the heavy weight it achieved low speeds and had limited cross-country capability.

The '88mm cannon is known for its revolutionary shell caliber that pierced the toughest armor like a tin can. Used in all over Europe during the World War 2, most famous places are Normandy (Op. Overlord) and all over Holland (Op. MarketGarden).

Mounted on a wheeled carriage, the Flak 38 gun was a further development of the Flak-30 AA gun: lighter, but boasting higher rate of fire. It was used by Wehrmacht, Luftwaffe and SS troops for anti-aircraft defence. It could, however, be easily employed against infantry and lightly-armored vehicles.

Serial production of GAZ-67 started in October 1943. Being notably heavier than its American counterparts, this Soviet 4WD car was not actually inferior to them in terms of mobility while its high cross-country ability, reliability and simplicity quickly brought the Ivan-Wyllis popularity among the soldiers and officers of the Red Army. This vehicle was widely used for transporting medium-ranking command staff and headquarters staff as well as for reconnaissance, communications and towing light artillery. On some modifications a vertical bar with a machine gun mount was installed.

Inside this truck you will find tools for repairing equipment, materials for building obstacles and defences and anti-personnel and anti-tank mines. Obstacles are usually built in front of occupied positions or sometimes on the flanks and in the gaps between them. Defences are made of sandbags and serve to strengthen the positions of friendly infantry.   This military truck was a modification to the ASKh-353 civilian vehicle. During the war the majority of these vehicles served to transport cargo, redeploy infantry and tow artillery. Some modifications may have been used as petrol tankers.

Inside this truck you will find a repair kit, small arms and light artillery ammo, grenades, mines and other ammunition.   This military truck was a modification of the ASKh-353 civilian vehicle. During the war the majority of these vehicles served to transport loads, redeploy infantry and tow artillery. Some modifications may have been used as petrol tankers.

An original multi-tier design made this American medium tank one of the most recognisable in the world. The right side of its hull housed a 75mm mortar gun, the second 45mm gun was mounted on the turret and above this was fitted another small cupola which held a machine gun. On the battlefield the tall hull of the General Lee proved to be too good a target for enemy guns and hence, despite its relatively powerful armament and armor, its production was stopped in 1942.
hamilcar Glider was used to transport Tetrach light tanks. Mainly used by the British Royal Commandos.

The production of these unsophisticated and cheaply produced tank destroyers started in March 1944 and continued until the end of the war. The 75mm AT gun PaK 39 was mounted on the chassis of a Czech Lt38 light tank, which gave the vehicle good mobility. Compact dimensions, low profile and sloped frontal armor resulted in increased shell resistance, but at the same time had a negative impact on the amount of carried ordnance. Despite insufficient side protection, the Hetzer is widely considered to be one of the most successful vehicles in its class.

This vehicle entered service with the Red Army on July 3, 1944 and was basically a further developed version of the SU-85. Thanks to high rate of fire and great ballistic properties of its new 100mm gun, which was based on a naval flak gun, it could destroy any enemy tank from medium and long distances. The tank's hull was welded from thick, sloping armor plates, and the chassis was taken from the T-34/85. The combination of great firepower, heavy armor and fair mobility made the SU-100 one of the best armored vehicles of the Great Patriotic War.
Dive bomber il-2 was so deadly and a pesky divebomber that always assured the death of Germans, eventually the German forces started calling it the white death.

This Soviet heavy tank entered production in October 1945 replacing the KV-85. Its very name, Iosif Stalin, implied that this machine should be a leader in its class and it managed to fulfil the hopes vested in it. While its weight was almost equal to that of its predecessors, the IS-1 boasted better protection and had an all-cast turret which housed an 85mm D-5T gun with a 48.8 calibre barrel length. The tank was used in offensive operations to break through fortified areas where it could operate under dense enemy fire relentlessly shattering the German defences. The weight of the machine had a negative impact on its ride characteristics but in such situations speed was of less important than robust armor and powerful armament.

The SdKfz 234 armored, all-wheel drive vehicle was mass produced in 1943. Thanks to sloping armor plates, the hull protected the crew not only from shell fragments and infantry weapons, but also from low-calibre artillery fire. Apart from that, the powerful engine allowed the vehicle to achieve high speeds, and its armament proved to be very effective against enemy infantry and lightly-armored vehicles. Thanks to that, the "Puma" rightfully deserves the title of the best armored car of WWII.

The IS-2 entered mass production in October 1943 and, with its long-barrelled 122mm gun able to destroy German tanks from a long range, was considered to be the most powerful Soviet tank of WWII. However, because of a separate ammo hold, the gun's reload time was disturbingly long. Against aircraft and lightly-armored targets the tank employed a turret-mounted large-calibre machine gun.

The Soviet heavy tank IS-3 is one of the strongest tanks of World War 2. The first machines in this series went into production in May 1945 and received a baptism by fire during the defeat of the Kwantung Army. When the IS-3 was designed, all the drawbacks of its predecessors were analysed in detail. The layout of the turret and the hull was upgraded and the position of the armor plates at the front was changed eventually making the machine almost invulnerable. Its 122mm gun destroyed the equipment and field fortifications of the enemy with the same effectiveness; however its separate loading system made reloading very slow. A DShK heavy anti-aircraft submachine gun mounted on the turret was successfully used against infantry as well as air and light armored land targets.

The ISU-152 heavy, self-propelled artillery piece entered service with the Red Army on November 6, 1943. In comparison to the former SU-152, it boasted better armor, a more reliable IS-1 tank chassis, and a great effective range of its on-board howitzer. However, the separate loading system had negative effect on the tank's rate of fire, thus degrading its capabilities in tank-to-tank combat. As a result, large-calibre HE rounds fired by the ISU-152 were mainly used to demolish fortifications and support advancing infantry. To protect the vehicle from close-range attack, it was equipped with a top-mounted large-calibre DShK machine gun.

The Jagdpanther was mass produced since February 1944 and used on all fronts until the end of the war. The chassis of the Panther tank was best suited for building a new tank destroyer. It was given a new cabin with good ballistic profile and a long-barrelled PaK 43/3 gun, which was able to penetrate the armor of any enemy tank even at long distances. Its formidable firepower, high mobility and low profile made the Jagdpanther one of the most powerful and renowned tank destroyers.

The design of this US-produced mortar was purchased from French engineer Edgar Brandt. The smoothbore tube rested upon a rectangular support plate and was supported by a simple two-legged mount - this standard scheme allowed the mortar to fire fragmentation, incendiary and illumination shells via a plunging trajectory. The firing was triggered by the shell primer descending upon a fixed pin inside the tube.

In the summer of 1944, the Wehrmacht received their heaviest tank destroyer ever - the Jagdtiger. Built on the King Tiger chassis, it had the drawback of being exceptionally heavy, which resulted in low mobility. However, as regarding armor and firepower, this vehicle was unmatched - its 128mm long-barrelled gun was able to destroy any adversary with ease, and the armor thickness reached as much as 250mm.

This armored half-track was manufactured in the USA to transport infantry and artillery. Its spacious body had an open design and as well as a compartment for 8 infantrymen it had a special mount with a heavy machine gun mounted on it. The M3 proved to be a fast and reliable vehicle very suitable for use in the harsh conditions of the war.
JU-52 Tanteju was used by the German Airborne

Soviet high-calibre machinegun, capable of destroying soft-skinned and low thickness armored vehicles aswell as engaging in anti-aircaft roles.   The high-calibre ShVAK machinegun was developed in 1944 and used by the Red Army's infantry, anti-aircraft and armor divisions. Weighing 161kg, it was rather heavy, therefore dictating the use of a wheeled mount for easier transportation. Combining high rate of fire and firepower, the ShVAK was effectively used against enemy infantry and light armor.

Soviet mass-produced heavy tank, built to withstand the most powerful or enemy armaments, this slow moving and slow firing vehicle is best deployed in static defensive positions to conserve fuel and protect is flanks.   World's first mass-produced tank with anti-artillery armor entered service with the Red Army on December 19, 1939. Until the arrival of German Tigers, the KV-1 was virtually invincible: its 76mm main gun was capable of defeating any enemy tank, while German guns could not penetrate its thick frontal armor at all.

The light 4x4 all-wheel drive SdKfz saw production from 1935 to 1944. It was mostly used for terrain reconnaissance ahead of tank columns. The petrol engine at the rear of the armored car enabled it to reach high speeds, but its relatively poor defences had a negative impact on its performance in open combat.

Soviet mass-produced Heavy 'behemoth tank, equipped with armor capable of withstanding direct artillery hits and sporting a massive 122mm main gun, this vehicle can blow away light vehicles and fortified positions with ease.   Entering service with the Red Army in the early 1940's, the KV-2 was virtually impervious to enemy anti-tank weapons, although, because of its low manoeuvrability and rate of fire, was mainly used as a siege weapon.

Entered service with the Red Army on August 8, 1943 and was actively used in battle throughout 1944. The KV85's low manoeuvrability was compensated by its thick armor and a powerful 85mm gun, which was capable of defeating almost all medium and heavy tanks.

Developed in 1944, the 32-barrelled Land Mattress multiple rocket launcher was initially intended for marine support and was used on British combat ships. This deadly gun turned out to be so effective during the Battle of Walcheren Island that it was immediately decided to start manufacture of its mobile ground-based modification. Dealing massive damage, its single volley was equally efficient to the fire of a howitzer battery. Perhaps the only drawback of this rocket launcher was its long reloading time.

This heavy field howitzer design was based on the old 155mm French guns and entered mass production in 1941. It was intended for indirect fire on enemy personnel, fortifications and important shallow objectives. The M114 proved to be an excellent tool on the battlefield, and its easy maintenance, good ballistics and sturdy construction earned the gun popularity among US artillery troops.

Experience of combat action in the first years of the war and the extremely high effectiveness of the Germans' mobile anti-aircraft guns made the American high command think about developing their own mobile anti-aircraft systems. An upgraded turret by Maxson, equipped with four combined Browning machine guns, was fitted to the chassis of the M3 multi-purpose armored vehicle and, by May 1943, the new vehicle had entered service with the US Army. Such AA systems were part of special anti-craft and artillery battalions and were equally effective at hitting enemy aircraft, infantry and light armored vehicles.

This 18-tonne Gun Motor Carriage was distinguished by its excellent speed and featured a powerful 76mm gun which was capable of destroying almost all enemy vehicles. The excellent mobility and low profile made the M18 a difficult target for enemy guns. However, due to their insufficient shell-proof capacity, these vehicles were forced to fire from under cover. Hellcats were also armed with high-calibre anti-aircraft machine guns and were actively used by the U.S. army in Italy and Northwestern Europe.

Soviet supply truck bearing ammunitions of artillery calibre, 105 - 155mm.   The 3-tonne Soviet ZIS-5 truck entered mass production in the early 1930s. Easy to maintain, it achieved relatively high speeds and was used during the war for transporting troops, cargo and towing artillery.

This self-propelled anti-aircraft gun was developed in 1945, and was primarily used for AA defence of vehicles on the move and in deployment sites. The M24 "Chaffee" chassis provided it with good speed and manoeuvrability, and two paired 40mm Bofors guns could engage not only planes, but also light and even medium enemy tanks. The first M19s were ready by the end of war, but did not see action.

This half-track armored vehicle was designed as a means of transport for artillery divisions and was produced by the US since 1941. Some vehicles were delivered to the USSR as part of the lend-lease program. Its roomy, open hull was protected by steel armor plates, and the powerful engine provided the vehicle with cross-country capability and good speed. The infantry compartment had 8 seats for fully equipped soldiers, and a special base housed a large-calibre Browning machine gun. The sides and rear of the vehicle had mounts for additional weapons.

This high-speed armored car was manufactured by Ford from March 1943 and was based on the M8 Greyhound. Its predecessor's rotating turret was replaced by a superstructure with a turret for a heavy M2HB machine gun. That left space for passenger seats and a powerful radio transmitter. A low degree of protection predetermined the use of M20 as a command and reconnaissance vehicle. However, despite this, the crew was also armed with a rocket launcher to fight enemy armored vehicles.

Entered service in the US Army in the summer of 1944 as a replacement for the M3 "Stuart", which was quickly becoming obsolete. In terms of firepower and armor the M24 surpassed all the light tanks of WWII. Despite its 75mm gun being ineffective against medium and heavy tanks, its great mobility allowed the "Chaffee" to be successfully used in scouting and airborne missions.

The heavily armed M26 Pershing entered production in November 1944. Its frontal armor could withstand hits from Tigers and Panthers and its long-barreled 90mm gun successfully destroyed enemy tanks at medium and long range. Its heavy weight had a negative impact on its speed, but overall the tank turned out be more effective than other US and British tanks.

American built multi-purpose armored troops transport, able to carry up to 12 fully laiden men aswell as tow cannons of the field-class type.   This armored half-truck was produced by the US since 1941 and used as a transport vehicle for tank corps and artillery divisions. Some vehicles were delivered to USSR as part of a lend-lease program. The spacious hull was made open-top. Along with a compartment for eight soldiers it housed a large-calibre machinegun and mounts for additional machineguns in the rear and on the sides. M3 proved to be a fast and reliable vehicle, well suited for use in harsh conditions of war.

The Maxim machine gun model 1910 on Sokolov mount was a heavy machine gun used by the Imperial Russian Army during World War I and the Red Army during World War II. It was adopted in 1910 and was derived from Hiram Maxim's Maxim gun, chambered for the standard Russian 7.62Ч54mmR rifle cartridge. The M1910 was mounted on a wheeled mount with a gun shield and was replaced in Soviet service by the SG-43 Goryunov which retained the wheeled and shielded carriage, starting in 1943. In addition to the main infantry version, there were aircraft mounted (PV-1) and naval variants.

Soviet standard field howitzer of 122mm calibre capable of high explosive, smoke and shrapnel rounds.   The legendary "Sorokopyatka" entered service with the Red Army on April 24, 1938 and was its main artillery gun during the early stages of war. High rate of fire, compact design and a low shield plate made it easily concealable, while high mobility allowed its operators to change positions quickly. After the appearance of new German tanks it became largely obsolete and was mainly used for infantry support and against lightly armored targets.

This light gun was mass produced since 1940 and became the standard issue AT weapon of US infantry during the early stages of the war. Having a relatively high rate of fire and fair mobility, it successfully engaged light vehicles and infantry, but the increasingly thick armor of German tanks quickly caused these guns to become obsolete.

This American medium tank was put into mass production in 1942. It was widely used on all battlefields and lend-leased in large quantities to the United States' allies. Thanks to its moulded case and composite armor, the M4A1 was as well-protected as the Soviet T-34, and had better ergonomics, a more spacious turret and good mobility. Its 75mm gun was effective against light and medium enemy vehicles, but the arrival of the Tigers and Panthers made engineers look at modernising it.

In 1941, in a short period of time, American engineers developed a reliable and efficient military off-roader named the "Willys". The vehicle received a positive response – the excellent speed and manoeuvrability made it one of the best in its class and the possibility of mounting a large-calibre machine gun on a vertical support meant that this car could be used for reconnaissance purposes.

Based on the performance of certain aspects of U.S. tanks, American engineers continued to modify and improve the M4, their principal middle tank. Thus, by the spring of 1944, the "General Sherman" had reached the peak of its development. Marked "(76)W", the vehicle featured an improved turret, reinforced front plating and a powerful long-barrelled 76mm anti-tank gun. These innovations meant that the new modification was a serious threat to enemy tanks.

In order to make the multiple rocket launcher Calliope mobile it was mounted on a M4 Sherman. Because of its low accuracy it was mainly used for suppressive fire against enemy infantry or clusters of vehicles. After firing its rockets the tank could be used in its primary role, which was the indisputable advantage in the design.

The MG-34 entered service with the Wehrmacht in 1934 and was used in hand, mounted, anti-aircraft and tank variants. An MG mounted on a tripod was able to fire at both ground and airborne targets. While it surpassed its Western counterparts in terms of rate of fire, continuous fire caused the machine gun's barrel to overheat quickly.

This special assault variant of the M4 medium tank was designed for breaking through fortified enemy defences. It entered service with the US Army in May 1944 where it got its nickname Jumbo. The thick armor of its turret and front hull made it almost invulnerable to enemy guns. However, at the same time, its increased weight had a negative impact on the speed and cross-country ability of the machine. Its 75mm gun could effectively hit firing posts, personnel and light and medium equipment, however it proved useless against German heavy tanks

In production since 1918, the SFH-18 heavy field howitzer was used by Wehrmacht troops during WWII against enemy artillery and personnel, as well as fortifications and trench lines. It fired 43kg HE rounds, capable of dealing devastating damage at very long distances, yet the gun's heavy weight impaired its mobility.

Refitted with the British 17-pounder gun the Sherman VC entered production in 1944 and was widely used by the Allies during the last months of the war. The high velocity of the new long-barreled anti-tank gun allowed it to penetrate armor as thick as 100mm. The tank's own armor was also enhanced. The Firefly performed well on the battlefield and a mounted large-calibre AA machine gun only further increased its efficiency.

In late 1940, US engineers started a project to adapt the 3-inch anti-aircraft gun T9 to an anti-tank role. The result was named M5 and entered service with the US Army in December 1942. Thanks to the high muzzle velocity of its round and excellent armor penetration capabilities this gun succeeded in replacing the early AT guns, quickly becoming ineffective against new German tanks.

Soviet mass-produced, highly successful and critically acclaimed medium tank. Capable of engaging the most well-armored of enemy vehicles, sporting a powerful 76mm cannon upon its first debut in 1941. 4 crew.   The first version of the famous T34 tank entered mass production on March 31st, 1940. Despite being relatively thin, its armor plates had a large slope angle, which increased the hull's resistance to enemy shelling, as well as the overall speed and mobility. As a result, the T-34, equal to Pz.Kpfw.III and Pz.Kpfw.IV in terms of armor and armament, turned out to be faster and more manoeuvrable.

Between 1941 and 1944, American Car and Foundry and Cadillac's Car Division manufactured a huge number of these light tanks which were to see action in the many theatres of World War 2. They were supplied to Great Britain, the Soviet Union, France, China and Yugoslavia. These low-weight, small machines boasted relatively good protection while the twin Cadillac automobile engines and an automatic gearbox provided the tank with perfect ride performance. At the same time a rather poor 37mm gun and insufficient protection prevented Stuarts from being a match for enemy medium and heavy equipment leaving them reconnaissance and direct infantry support missions.

This self-propelled artillery gun was mass-produced since April 1942 and mainly used for infantry support role. The 105mm field howitzer was mounted upon the chassis of a medium M3 tank, reinforcing the armament with a large-calibre AA machine gun. The impressive firepower of the main gun was supplemented by thick armor and excellent manoeuvrability for its class. The only shortcoming of the Priest was the open turret that left the crew vulnerable.

Soviet motorcycle, comparable in performance to the American Harley Davidson. Able to carry 3 fully laiden soldiers.   The M72 "Dnepr" army motorcycles entered mass production in 1941, following a decision to form motorcycle troops within the Red Army. The model equipped with a sidecar was armed with a 7.62mm DP machine gun and earned the soldiers' respect for being reliable and fast.

This reliable and undemanding all-terrain jeep was manufactured for the US Army from 1941. Thanks to its excellent ride performance and high cross-country ability, the Willys quickly gained popularity among American military personnel. On some models, a special vertical bar was installed with a pair of rocket grenade launchers mounted on it. This feature meant that the vehicle could be used as an auxiliary tool providing fire support to the troops by fighting enemy armored vehicles.

A light self-propelled gun built on an M5 tank chassis, produced since 1942. Mounted in an open turret, the 75mm gun was not effective against enemy tanks, however it performed well when used for infantry support. The open top, which left the crew vulnerable, and the weak armor were somewhat compensated for with good speed and manoeuvrability. Towards the end of 1944, the medium Sherman tank completely replaced the M8 Scott on the battlefield.

The first version of the Pz.IV assault tank turned out to be ineffective against Soviet T34s and KVs. However, by the spring of 1942, the Wehrmacht started receiving new versions of PzKpfw IV tanks with upgraded armament and long-barrelled anti-tank Kwk40 guns, capable of defeating almost any opponent. In addition, the tank had good manoeuvrability, which - along with the strong armor and powerful gun - turned it into a fearsome combat vehicle.

The Greyhound entered service with the US Army in early 1943 and became the most widespread armored car of WWII. The entirely welded hull was constructed from sloped steel plates, but the thin armor provided protection only against small firearms. The 37mm gun did not pose much of a threat to serious opponents, however thanks to its light weight and all-wheeled drive the vehicle boasted excellent speed and handling, which resulted in its high popularity with the troops.
